extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and commentators on trade and monetary policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying argumentative criteria from a classical political-economy exposition about free trade, import restraints, balance of trade, coinage, and banks (Adam Smith-style). Useful for evaluating trade policy proposals and monetary institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore freedom of trade gradually
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom of trade should be restored only by slow gradations, and with a good deal of reserve and circumspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not remove high duties and prohibitions all at once because cheap foreign goods might flood the home market and deprive many people of employment and subsistence. Introduce liberalization slowly with long warnings to allow adjustment of capital and labour; sudden removal risks considerable disorder and loss for undertakers with fixed capital in workhouses and instruments of trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess vulnerability by export orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufactures of which any part is commonly exported to other European countries without a bounty could be very little affected by the freest importation of foreign goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a domestic manufacture already competes in foreign markets without bounties, it must be competitively priced and will likely retain the home market despite imports. Identify which branches (e.g., woollens, tanned leather, hardware) are export-oriented and therefore less threatened by freer imports; luxury or non-exported manufactures (e.g., some silk/linen) are more vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect labour reallocation after trade liberalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Though people might be thrown out of their ordinary employment, it would by no means follow that they would be thereby deprived either of employment or subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical analogies (e.g., disbanding soldiers and seamen) to argue that many displaced workers will find other occupations over time. Consider differences in habits: manufacturers accustomed to industry adapt more easily to new trades than soldiers accustomed to pay and idleness. Account for collateral and seasonal employment and regional mobility when projecting employment impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove legal barriers to labour mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down the exclusive privileges of corporations, repeal the statute of apprenticeship, and repeal the law of settlements so a poor workman may seek employment elsewhere without fear of prosecution or removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy reforms that increase the natural liberty to exercise any industry will facilitate adjustment to trade liberalization. Removing institutional constraints on occupational and geographic mobility reduces structural unemployment risk from market opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about political obstacles to full free trade
rubrics_metrics.description: To expect that the freedom of trade should ever be entirely restored in Great Britain is as absurd as to expect that an Oceana or Utopia should ever be established in it; prejudices of the public and private interests of many individuals irresistibly oppose it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that entrenched private interests and popular prejudices will resist liberalization. Monopolies and large industrial interests can intimidate legislators and mobilize workmen; political economy prescriptions must account for distributional and political constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect fixed capital and provide long warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: The part of capital fixed in workhouses and in the instruments of trade could scarce be disposed of without considerable loss; equitable regard to his interest requires that changes of this kind should never be introduced suddenly, but slowly, gradually, and after a very long warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design transition policies that mitigate losses for capital-intensive producers — phased implementation, compensation mechanisms, or long lead times — to preserve fairness and reduce social disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tariffs intended to prevent importation
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes imposed with a view to prevent, or even to diminish importation, are evidently as destructive of the revenue of the customs as of the freedom of trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate taxes for revenue from protective tariffs. Using import duties primarily to block imports undermines both trade freedom and customs revenue; fiscal policy should not be disguised as protectionism if the aim is revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base import restraints solely on bilateral balance fears
rubrics_metrics.description: To lay extraordinary restraints upon the importation of goods of almost all kinds from those particular countries with which the balance of trade is supposed to be disadvantageous is unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if bilateral balance favors the other country, imports of cheaper/better goods can reduce overall import value and benefit consumers; consider substitution effects and possible re-exports. Resist blanket restraints motivated only by a presumed unfavourable bilateral balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider re-export and transit trade effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A great part of them might be re-exported to other countries, where, being sold with profit, they might bring back a return equal in value to the prime cost of the whole foreign goods imported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the intermediary role a country can play (like the Dutch carrying French goods) — imports may generate export re-shipments and associated earnings that offset apparent deficits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat customs records as unreliable for measuring balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The custom-house books ... are a very uncertain criterion, on account of the inaccuracy of the valuation at which the greater part of goods are rated in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely uncritically on customs valuations to measure trade balances; valuations may be inaccurate or manipulated. Use complementary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about using course of exchange to infer trade balances
rubrics_metrics.description: The course of exchange is, perhaps, almost equally so [an uncertain criterion].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exchange rates reflect debts/credits among many places and practices (bank money vs currency), not just bilateral trade flows; they can be influenced by third-country transactions and financial arrangements, so infer trade balances with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for differences between computed and real exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: The real exchange may be, and in fact often is, so very different from the computed one, that, from the course of the latter, no certain conclusion can ... be drawn concerning that of the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computed exchange (based on mint standards) can be misleading because actual circulating coin differs in wear, clipping, and intrinsic metal content; adjust measurements for the real metal content and circulation practices before concluding about balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider mint standards and coinage practices when comparing currencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the current coin of every country, compared with that of any other country, is in proportion ... to that which it actually does contain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing currencies, account for differences in how worn or clipped coins are relative to mint standards and for whether coinage costs are borne by the government or private individuals (which affects nominal vs real value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the effect of coinage charges on relative currency value
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries the expense of coinage is defrayed by the government; in others, it is defrayed by the private people ... In France a duty of eight per cent. is deducted for the coinage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where coinage incurs charges (e.g., minting fees), nominal sums in that currency may carry additional implicit value that must be compensated in exchange rates; adjust for coinage duties when judging parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for bank money (agio) versus common currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Bank money ... is always of more value than the same nominal sum of common currency. The difference between them is called the agio of the bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize bank money's premium: it is more secure, transferable by book entry, and used for foreign bills, so computed exchange can favor places paying in bank money even if real exchange favors the place paying in common currency. Distinguish types of money used to settle foreign bills when interpreting exchange and balance signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use banks of deposit to stabilize exchange in small states
rubrics_metrics.description: Small states ... have frequently enacted that foreign bills of exchange ... should be paid ... by a transfer in the books of a certain bank ... this bank being always obliged to pay, in good and true money, exactly according to the standard of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a trusted bank of deposit that pays in money of standard quality reduces uncertainty in foreign bills, creates demand for bank money, and can correct disadvantages from having mixed degraded currency. The Amsterdam bank example shows how such an institution reduces exchange uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the economic functions of bank credit and receipts
rubrics_metrics.description: The bank received coin ... gave a credit in its books called bank money ... and granted a recipice or receipt entitling the person ... to take out the bullion again ... (with a small keeping fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that banks' credits and receipts create tradable instruments: bank money (book credit) and receipts (claim on bullion) can be bought and sold; the agio reflects real advantages (security, transferability, ability to pay foreign bills). Bank pricing (bank price vs mint vs market) and storage/keeping charges affect behaviour of depositors and the liquidity of bullion markets.
